memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. "This time I have sinned," he said to them. "The Lord is in the right, and I and my people are in the wrong. Pray to the Lord, for we have had enough thunder and hail. I will let you go; you don't have to stay any longer."" - Exodus 9:27-28 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
These are the strongest words Pharaoh has ever spoken. I have sinned. The Lord is in the right. I am in the wrong.

If you heard that from someone, you would call it repentance. And yet, within a few verses, he takes it all back.

That tells us something important. Saying the right words is not the same as a changed heart. Pharaoh confessed under a hailstorm, and his confession lasted exactly as long as the storm.

Paul distinguishes between godly sorrow, which leads to repentance and salvation, and worldly sorrow, which is really just regret about consequences (2 Cor 7:10). One person weeps because they have grieved God. Another weeps because they got caught.

This is worth examining honestly, without becoming morbid. Real repentance changes direction, not just vocabulary. It survives the end of the pressure.

Notice too what Pharaoh actually asks for: enough thunder and hail. He wants the storm stopped, not his heart changed. That is the tell.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. When I confess sin, am I sorry for the sin or for the consequences?
2. Has any recent repentance of mine changed how I actually live?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Lord, give me true repentance, not just regret. Change my direction, not only my words. Amen.
